query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, brittle behavior can emerge not from pre‐existing, equilibrium grain-boundary precipitates or impurity segregation but via dynamic nanoclustering of selected principal elements at high-angle grain boundaries during high-strain-rate deformation. This dynamic clustering lowers grain boundary cohesion (e.g., by initiating cavitation) and creates localized sites for brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with no significant pre-existing grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled high-strain-rate deformation (e.g., sliding contact or shear testing) in an ultra-high vacuum environment where thermal effects and oxidation are minimized.
generation.conditions: Room temperature, ultra-high vacuum, high strain-rate loading (with minimal temperature rise) to avoid thermal-triggered diffusion effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic nanoclustering of specific elements (such as Cr, Ni, and Mn) at high-angle grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During high-strain-rate deformation, severe local shear leads to the dynamic clustering of selected principal elements at grain boundaries. This nanoclustering reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries and promotes cavitation (nano-porosity formation) which serves as the nucleation sites for intergranular cracks and brittle fracture. This mechanism is distinct from conventional alloys where equilibrium grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation dominates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample deformed under low strain-rate or thermally equilibrated conditions, the high-strain-rate deformed HEA will exhibit localized nanoscale compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries, increased cavitation (nanoporosity) along these boundaries, and a corresponding reduction in toughness, evidenced by earlier onset of intergranular cracking.
generation.baseline: An initially homogeneous, single-phase HEA without observable grain-boundary nanoclusters or intermetallic precipitates when tested under conditions that do not induce dynamic clustering (e.g., low strain-rate deformation).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be active under high-strain-rate, low thermal-load conditions in environments that preclude equilibrium segregation or oxidation effects; it may not apply if significant thermal diffusion or impurity-driven segregation occurs.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical strain rate, the size and distribution of the nanoclusters required to significantly lower grain-boundary cohesion, and the universality of this mechanism across different HEA compositions remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase HEA samples with similar microstructures. Deform one set under high-strain-rate conditions (using, e.g., high-speed sliding or shear testing in ultra-high vacuum) and the other under controlled, low-strain-rate conditions. Use atom probe tomography (APT) or high-resolution TEM to characterize grain-boundary composition before and after deformation. Correlate the presence (or absence) of nanoscale clusters at grain boundaries with fracture toughness measurements.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and nanocluster formation via APT or HR-TEM
Quantitative measurement of cavitation (nano-porosity) along grain boundaries
Fracture toughness (e.g., using micro-tensile testing) and ductility assessment
Strain rate and temperature monitoring during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-strain-rate deformation does not lead to detectable dynamic nanoclustering at grain boundaries, or if the samples exhibiting nanoclustering do not show a measurable reduction in toughness relative to low-strain-rate controls, then the hypothesis that dynamic nanoclustering governs brittle behavior in the HEA will be falsified.

Recent work has shown that low friction of bare metals, in the range μ≅0.2−0.5, can be explained as the dynamic softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) of surfaces due to highly surface-localized, shear-induced severe plastic deformation,,. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys.
